paragraphs: This paper studies how learning from several labeled tasks can help a model resist adversarial attacks on a new task. The goal is transfer with low robust error: predictions should remain reliable under attacks at inference time, even when the target task has little training data. The question is therefore about transferring protection as well as predictive ability.

The analysis assumes that source and target tasks share a useful representation, with each task requiring only a linear predictor on top. Under this shared structure, the authors derive bounds on excess adversarial transfer risk for two classes of losses: Lipschitz losses and smooth nonnegative losses. These bounds describe the error associated with learning a robust predictor rather than having an ideal one available.

The resulting rates support adversarially training representations across diverse tasks as a way to improve protection in data-scarce settings. This is a theoretical conclusion within the stated representation and loss assumptions. The paper also establishes new rates for learning a single task, connecting its transfer analysis to the simpler setting without multiple source tasks.
neurips-2024-adversarially-robust-multi-.tldr: Under shared-representation assumptions, theoretical bounds show how adversarial training across diverse tasks can improve robustness on a new task with limited data.

paragraphs: AlphaTablets addresses the reconstruction of flat surfaces in three dimensions from video recorded by a single camera. A useful plane representation must capture both a continuous surface and its boundary. The paper represents each plane as a rectangle with an alpha channel, allowing the rectangular support to describe a surface whose visible extent has a more precise outline.

The reconstruction pipeline builds these representations from the bottom up. It starts with small image regions called superpixels and geometric information supplied by pretrained models. These provide initial 3D planes, which are then refined through differentiable rendering: rendering the planes into images provides a route for adjusting their parameters. A merging procedure lets individual AlphaTablets grow and become more complete.

Alternating optimization and merging produces planes with solid surfaces and clear boundaries. On ScanNet, the authors report state-of-the-art performance for 3D planar reconstruction. The contribution combines a representation with a reconstruction procedure, while the broader possibility of using AlphaTablets in other applications remains a proposed opportunity rather than the reported benchmark result.
neurips-2024-alphatablets-a-generic-plan.tldr: AlphaTablets represents 3D planes as rectangles with transparency and refines them through rendering and merging to reconstruct planar surfaces from monocular video.

paragraphs: Steering vectors adjust a language model’s behavior during inference by intervening on its internal activations. Their appeal is that they offer an efficient way to influence capabilities or alignment. This paper investigates whether those interventions behave reliably across inputs and whether their effects carry over to prompts outside the distribution in which they were developed.

Even within the original distribution, the authors find that steerability varies substantially from one input to another. For some concepts, incidental biases make a substantial contribution to apparent steering effectiveness. This means that success on a collection of inputs does not establish that an intervention will guide behavior equally well on other inputs from the same distribution.

Outside that distribution, the picture is mixed: steering vectors often transfer well, but several concepts are sensitive to reasonable prompt changes. Those changes can cause generalization to fail. The findings support a conditional view of steering: it can work well under suitable circumstances, while input variability and prompt sensitivity remain obstacles to dependable use at scale.
neurips-2024-analysing-the-generalisatio.tldr: Steering vectors can guide language models effectively, but their effects vary across inputs and can break under reasonable prompt changes.

paragraphs: Text-to-video models can produce impressive results while still missing a prompt’s meaning or generating visually unappealing videos. Preference-based feedback offers a way to improve these qualities, but collecting human judgments is expensive. This paper investigates whether multimodal language models can supply useful video preference annotations and help address the shortage of comprehensive preference datasets.

The authors first compare model-generated annotations with human judgments and find a high degree of agreement. Building on that result, they use multimodal language models to create fine-grained annotations across two dimensions. The resulting dataset, VideoPrefer, contains 135,000 preference annotations. Agreement with people motivates using this feedback source; the finding does not claim that the two sources are interchangeable in every case.

Using VideoPrefer, the authors introduce VideoRM, a general-purpose reward model for preferences over text-generated videos. It provides a learned means of evaluating video preferences within this setting. Their experiments support the effectiveness of both the dataset and reward model, establishing a practical feedback resource for efforts to align video generation with human preferences.
neurips-2024-boosting-text-to-video-gene.tldr: The paper uses multimodal language-model feedback to build VideoPrefer and train VideoRM, supported by strong agreement between generated annotations and human video preferences.

paragraphs: Long robotic tasks are difficult because small mistakes can accumulate as a robot acts. An open-loop system follows its plan without the real-time feedback needed to correct those deviations. CLOVER introduces a closed-loop approach in which an imagined visual plan provides a reference, and feedback helps the robot adjust its actions as the task unfolds.

The framework has three connected components. A text-conditioned video diffusion model generates visual plans describing expected progress. A measurable embedding space supports quantifying the difference between the reference and observed state. A feedback-driven controller then uses that error information to refine actions and trigger a new plan when needed. This links visual generation to ongoing control through an explicit error signal.

The authors report improvements on real-world robotic tasks and state-of-the-art performance on CALVIN, with an 8% improvement over earlier open-loop counterparts. These findings support the value of checking progress against generated expectations during execution. The contribution is the combination of visual planning, measurable feedback, and action correction for more adaptive manipulation.
neurips-2024-closed-loop-visuomotor-cont.tldr: CLOVER uses generated video plans and measurable visual feedback to correct robotic actions and replan, improving long-horizon manipulation performance.

paragraphs: This paper examines how progress is measured in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning. Its central concern is that inconsistent baselines and evaluation procedures make it hard to tell whether a new algorithm represents a real improvement. The authors begin with a representative study of published work, identifying substantial shortcomings in how proposed methods have been assessed.

They then implement simple baselines carefully and compare them directly with prior results. Across 47 datasets used in earlier work, these baselines match or exceed the reported state of the art on 35, or almost 75%. In many cases, they substantially outperform more elaborate algorithms. This demonstrates that the strength of the comparison method can materially change the apparent contribution of a new technique.

The authors also provide a standardized evaluation methodology, baseline implementations, and statistically robust results across several scenarios. These resources give future work a more consistent basis for comparison. The broader implication is that stronger experimental foundations could improve the reliability of progress claims, without requiring evaluation procedures that are difficult for researchers to adopt.
neurips-2024-dispelling-the-mirage-of-pr.tldr: Carefully implemented simple baselines match or beat reported offline MARL leaders on 35 of 47 datasets, motivating standardized evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper studies the efficiency of first-price auctions when participants have different objectives. Traditional bidders maximize utility, while autobidders maximize value. The authors analyze the price of anarchy, which captures how inefficient the resulting outcomes can be compared with an optimal allocation. The focus is on theoretical efficiency guarantees across different bidder populations.

When every participant is an autobidder, the paper establishes a price of anarchy of one-half. When traditional bidders and autobidders participate together, the guarantee falls to approximately 0.457, with the exact value specified through an optimization problem. These results complement the previously established traditional-bidder value of one minus one over e squared. Thus, changing the mix of objectives can weaken the auction’s worst-case efficiency guarantee.

The authors also study a setting in which the seller can use machine-learned advice. As the accuracy of that advice increases, the price of anarchy improves smoothly from approximately 0.457 to one. This result links better advice to a stronger efficiency guarantee within the studied setting; it does not assert that arbitrary learned advice always delivers optimal outcomes.
neurips-2024-efficiency-of-the-first-pri.tldr: First-price auctions have weaker worst-case efficiency with mixed bidder objectives, while increasingly accurate machine-learned advice can improve the guarantee.

paragraphs: Retraining a model’s final layer offers an efficient way to correct an existing predictor for subgroup fairness. However, these corrections can be vulnerable to incorrect training labels. This paper targets that weakness by introducing a label-noise correction that can be added to last-layer retraining methods, preserving the appeal of making a relatively small model adjustment.

The approach uses label spreading on a nearest-neighbor graph built in the model’s latent representation. In plain terms, examples are connected according to their similarity in the learned feature space, and label information is spread through those connections. This makes relationships among represented examples part of the correction procedure, addressing noise in the labels used for retraining.

The authors report state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy across a broad range of symmetric label noise and multiple datasets containing spurious correlations. Worst-group accuracy focuses attention on the subgroup with the weakest performance. The method adds minimal computational overhead relative to existing approaches, suggesting that improved robustness can be incorporated without losing the efficiency motivating last-layer correction.
neurips-2024-enhancing-robustness-of-las.tldr: Spreading labels through a latent nearest-neighbor graph improves the robustness of last-layer fairness corrections under symmetric label noise with little added computation.

paragraphs: Language models can memorize training material and produce similar content later. This paper studies copyright takedowns: attempts to prevent a model from generating particular copyrighted content. The technical challenge includes retaining useful factual knowledge and general capabilities while suppressing the targeted material. The authors introduce CoTaEval to evaluate these competing objectives together.

CoTaEval assesses takedown effectiveness, retention of uncopyrightable facts found in the targeted content, general utility, and efficiency. The study examines interventions at several points: system prompts that instruct the model, filters applied during generation, and unlearning approaches that change what the model has learned. Evaluating them through the same framework makes their different effects easier to compare.

No examined method performs best across all evaluated dimensions. The findings therefore reveal unresolved tradeoffs in the tested approaches, rather than establishing a universally effective takedown mechanism. The paper frames these results as motivation for further research and as evidence of potential technical challenges for policy proposals that depend on such capabilities. Its contribution is an evaluation framework and a comparative assessment of feasibility and side effects.
neurips-2024-evaluating-copyright-takedo.tldr: CoTaEval finds that existing copyright-takedown approaches face tradeoffs between suppressing targeted content, preserving facts, maintaining utility, and efficiency.

paragraphs: Fair GLASSO addresses fairness in Gaussian graphical models, where a graph represents statistical relationships among variables. The paper focuses on sensitive attributes associated with nodes and on imbalances between groups. It introduces two bias measures that encourage balance in statistical similarities across those groups, making the intended notion of fairness part of the model-estimation problem.

The method adds fairness regularization to graphical lasso, which estimates sparse Gaussian precision matrices. These matrices describe the dependency structure the model learns. An efficient proximal gradient algorithm computes the estimates. By incorporating the proposed bias measures into estimation, the method makes group balance an explicit objective alongside the accuracy and sparsity of the resulting graphical model.

The theoretical analysis describes the tradeoff between fairness and estimation accuracy, including conditions under which adding fairness regularization can preserve accuracy. It also analyzes computational complexity and establishes fast convergence for the algorithm. Synthetic and real-world simulations support the approach’s effectiveness. The fairness claim is tied to the proposed statistical measures, and accuracy preservation is a conditional result.
neurips-2024-fair-glasso-estimating-fair.tldr: Fair GLASSO adds group-balance penalties to sparse Gaussian graphical-model estimation and analyzes when fairness improvements can preserve accuracy.

paragraphs: Fisher-Flow develops a geometric approach to generating discrete data, such as biological sequences. The paper starts from categorical probability distributions and treats them as points in a space whose geometry is defined by the Fisher–Rao metric. This provides a way to describe continuous movement between distributions even though the eventual data consists of discrete choices.

The construction reparameterizes the problem on the positive portion of a hypersphere. On that surface, the authors can use geodesics with closed-form expressions to transport probability mass from a source distribution toward a target. Riemannian optimal transport can further improve the learned flows’ training dynamics. The authors also prove an optimality property for the induced gradient flow in reducing forward KL divergence.

Experiments cover synthetic problems and several real-world benchmarks, including DNA promoter and enhancer sequence design. Fisher-Flow improves over prior diffusion and flow-matching models on these evaluations. These empirical gains support the usefulness of matching the flow to the geometry of categorical probabilities; the theoretical optimality claim specifically concerns the stated divergence-reduction property.
neurips-2024-fisher-flow-matching-for-ge.tldr: Fisher-Flow uses the geometry of categorical probabilities to generate discrete data, improving over evaluated diffusion and flow-matching alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper asks how neural networks can represent combinations of meaningful parts while retaining continuous, distributed representations. Conventional disentanglement approaches often express compositional structure through separately arranged components. The authors argue that this creates tension with deep learning’s distributed foundations and investigate a more flexible way to encode that structure.

Their proposal, Soft Tensor Product Representation, extends the Tensor Product Representation framework. Soft TPR encodes compositional information in a distributed form, and a dedicated Soft TPR Autoencoder learns these representations. The representation and learning architecture are developed together, so the model is explicitly designed to support this approach to organizing visual information.

Across visual representation-learning evaluations, the framework outperforms conventional disentanglement alternatives. The authors report state-of-the-art disentanglement, improved convergence of representation learning, and better sample efficiency and performance when downstream training data is scarce. These results support the practical promise of distributed compositional representations. The broader suggestion that this form better aligns with deep learning’s foundations remains an interpretation of the approach and findings.
neurips-2024-fully-distributed-flexible-.tldr: Soft TPR learns flexible, distributed compositional visual representations that improve disentanglement and downstream sample efficiency in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Vector quantization represents an image as a sequence of discrete codes selected from a learned codebook. These codes support image generation, but codebooks trained only on images may transfer poorly to tasks involving language. LG-VQ addresses this mismatch by incorporating text knowledge while learning the codebook, aiming to make the image codes more compatible with textual meaning.

The framework begins with semantic knowledge from a pretrained text model. It then uses two components, a Semantic Alignment Module and a Relationship Alignment Module, to transfer that knowledge into the codes. Together, these modules target alignment between the learned codebook and text. The approach is model-agnostic, allowing it to be incorporated into existing vector-quantization models.

The authors report improved performance on image reconstruction and multiple multimodal downstream tasks. This matters because the intervention affects the representation those tasks use: language guidance enters when the discrete image vocabulary is learned. The reported results support using that guidance to improve both reconstruction and tasks that require images and text to work together.
neurips-2024-lg-vq-language-guided-codeb.tldr: LG-VQ transfers pretrained text knowledge into image codebooks to improve reconstruction and multimodal downstream performance.

paragraphs: Adaptive Text-Image Harmony tackles the creation of a new object image from an object description and an existing object image. Diffusion models can struggle to combine these inputs because one dominates the output. The paper aims to preserve meaningful contributions from both, producing an object that integrates the textual concept with information from the reference image.

ATIH introduces controls at several points in generation. A scale factor balances text and image features in cross-attention, while an injection step preserves image information in self-attention during inversion. A balanced loss with a noise parameter addresses the tension between making the image editable and retaining fidelity to it. These controls target different parts of the same integration problem.

The method adjusts its parameters using a similarity score that rewards agreement with both inputs while also balancing those agreements. This makes harmony between the two inputs an explicit selection criterion. Extensive experiments support the approach’s effectiveness, including unusual creations such as a colobus–glass jar combination. The stated outcome is more successful integration of the supplied object text and image.
neurips-2024-novel-object-synthesis-via-.tldr: ATIH adaptively balances text and image influences in diffusion generation to create novel objects that reflect both inputs.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when discovering how similar two elements are requires a costly, noisy query. The goal is to group the elements while asking as few questions as possible. Because each answer is only a noisy sample of weighted similarity, the algorithm must manage uncertainty as well as decide which relationships deserve further measurement.

The authors formulate two versions of the problem using pure exploration in combinatorial multi-armed bandits. One works with a fixed confidence requirement; the other works with a fixed query budget. For each setting, they combine a strategy for sampling pairwise similarities with a classic approximation algorithm for correlation clustering, and analyze the resulting guarantees.

The contribution also concerns computational feasibility. The underlying offline optimization problem is NP-hard, yet the proposed procedures run in polynomial time. The authors identify these as the first such results for this class of pure-exploration problems with an NP-hard offline component. Using approximation makes it possible to connect query allocation with tractable clustering without claiming an efficient exact solution to the hard optimization problem.
neurips-2024-query-efficient-correlation.tldr: The paper combines adaptive similarity sampling with approximate correlation clustering to obtain polynomial-time guarantees under confidence or query-budget constraints.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks often struggle to learn long-term memories, a difficulty commonly associated with gradients becoming too small or too large. The success of state-space models, which are a subclass of recurrent networks, motivates this paper to examine what else makes training difficult. Its analysis identifies a sensitivity problem that can persist without exploding gradients.

As a network’s memory increases, changes to its parameters can produce increasingly large changes in its outputs. Gradient-based learning therefore becomes sensitive because an update can strongly alter the network’s behavior. This provides an additional explanation for training difficulty beyond the usual account based only on whether gradients vanish or explode.

The authors find that element-wise recurrence, combined with careful parameterization, helps mitigate this effect. This design pattern appears in state-space models and in other architectures, including LSTMs. The result offers an explanation for some differences in trainability across recurrent architectures. It also makes the combination of recurrence structure and parameterization central to understanding how networks can maintain longer memories while remaining easier to optimize.
neurips-2024-recurrent-neural-networks-v.tldr: Longer recurrent memory can amplify output sensitivity to parameter changes even without exploding gradients, while element-wise recurrence and careful parameterization help mitigate it.

paragraphs: Adders and multipliers influence both the speed and physical footprint of hardware systems. ArithTreeRL searches for better designs by treating arithmetic structure construction as a single-player tree-generation game. Reinforcement learning guides this construction, giving the search a structured way to explore the many possible arrangements of an arithmetic unit.

The authors report finding improved designs within a few hours. For 128-bit adders, their method discovers designs that are Pareto optimal under theoretical metrics, reflecting the tradeoff between speed and size. Relative to PrefixRL, reported delay reductions reach 26% and size reductions reach 30%. These are up-to improvements, so they describe the strongest reported gains rather than a uniform reduction for every design.

For multipliers, the paper reports speed improvements of as much as 49% and size reductions of as much as 45% compared with RL-MUL. It also reports integration into 7nm technology. Together, the results support tree generation as a useful search formulation for both arithmetic modules, with the method’s scalability and flexibility extending beyond a single design type.
neurips-2024-scalable-and-effective-arit.tldr: ArithTreeRL uses reinforcement learning to generate arithmetic trees, finding faster and smaller adder and multiplier designs in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper approaches language-model compression as a search over architectures. Many compression methods focus on changing weights, while conventional architecture search is difficult to apply to very large models. The authors propose a training-free framework that searches for smaller subnetworks within an existing language model, aiming to preserve its strengths while making inference faster.

The selected subnetworks inherit particular weights from the original model. The method then applies a reformation algorithm that uses information from omitted weights to adjust the retained ones, requiring only a small amount of calibration data. This gives the removed weights a role in constructing the final compact model, beyond deciding which parts of the original network remain.

Compared with state-of-the-art training-free structured pruning methods, the approach achieves better performance across standard benchmarks. The resulting subnetworks also directly reduce GPU memory use and accelerate inference. These findings support architecture selection together with weight reformation as a practical compression strategy, connecting the quality of the smaller model to both its structure and its inherited parameters.
neurips-2024-search-for-efficient-large-.tldr: Training-free architecture search and calibration-based weight reformation produce smaller language models with improved benchmark performance over compared structured-pruning methods.

paragraphs: SemFlow connects two visual tasks: assigning semantic categories to image pixels and generating an image from a semantic mask. The paper treats them as reverse directions of one problem. This perspective motivates a shared model that transports between the distribution of real images and the distribution of masks, bringing perception and generation into a common framework.

The authors train an ordinary differential equation model motivated by rectified flow. Its symmetric training objective supports movement in both directions between images and masks. For segmentation, this addresses the mismatch between random diffusion outputs and the desired unique segmentation result. The same framework can run in the opposite direction to synthesize images from semantic layouts.

Image synthesis also needs variation: a semantic layout can support diverse appearances. SemFlow introduces a finite perturbation approach to increase this diversity without changing semantic categories. Experiments show competitive performance on both segmentation and semantic image synthesis. The findings support the feasibility of unifying these tasks, while the proposed perturbations accommodate the different output requirements of generation and segmentation.
neurips-2024-semflow-binding-semantic-se.tldr: SemFlow uses reversible rectified-flow transport between images and semantic masks to perform both segmentation and image synthesis.

paragraphs: Neural network interatomic potentials predict atomic energies and forces as surrogates for quantum-mechanical calculations. This paper investigates how to scale them efficiently. The authors argue that increasingly elaborate physical constraints can restrict scaling and may eventually limit performance, motivating a systematic study of architectures that gain expressivity as computational resources and data increase.

Their findings lead to EScAIP, a graph neural network using multi-head self-attention over neighbor-level representations. Optimized GPU attention kernels support its implementation. Compared with existing interatomic-potential models, the authors report at least a tenfold inference speedup and fivefold lower memory use. They also report state-of-the-art performance on datasets covering catalysts, molecules, and materials, including OC20, OC22, SPICE, and MPTrj.

To examine rotational behavior, they compare predicted forces on unseen atomic systems before and after rotation. The predictions exactly match the rotated forces in this test, which they interpret as evidence that the model learned rotational equivariance. This empirical finding supports their scaling approach. They present EScAIP as a proof of concept for a broader design philosophy toward general-purpose interatomic potentials.
neurips-2024-the-importance-of-being-sca.tldr: EScAIP uses scalable attention to improve interatomic-potential accuracy and efficiency, with rotation tests suggesting that it learned equivariant force predictions.

paragraphs: Sparse models aim to reduce memory and computation by keeping fewer active parameters. Successful neural-network pruning heuristics often draw on Optimal Brain Surgeon, which uses loss curvature to decide how to remove weights. This paper connects that idea to sparse recovery algorithms, seeking both stronger theoretical foundations and more effective practical optimization.

The central change is to use curvature information during the projection step of iterative sparse recovery methods such as iterative hard thresholding. That step determines a sparse version of the current solution. Incorporating second-order information makes the decision sensitive to how parameter changes affect the loss. The authors derive new algorithms from this connection between pruning and sparse recovery.

Under suitable assumptions in well-behaved settings, the algorithms have improved convergence bounds, and experiments show stronger practical convergence. The authors also extend the approach to training accurate sparse deep neural networks and validate those extensions at scale. The theoretical guarantees remain conditional, while the empirical results support the usefulness of curvature-aware sparse updates beyond the initial analytical setting.
neurips-2024-the-iterative-optimal-brain.tldr: Using loss curvature in sparse-recovery projection steps improves convergence guarantees under suitable assumptions and strengthens practical sparse-model training.

paragraphs: Speech recognition from audio, visual input, and their combination is often handled by separate models. Even joint research efforts can leave separate inference pipelines, with duplicated components and increased memory requirements. This paper develops training strategies that let a single model perform all three tasks, unifying the recognition system across the available input types.

The authors find that joint training improves visual and audiovisual recognition and overcomes typical optimization difficulties encountered when training from scratch. They also introduce greedy pseudo-labeling to make better use of unlabeled samples. A further self-supervised pretraining method operates within the same framework, and the paper demonstrates its effectiveness alongside the semi-supervised approach.

On LRS3, the unified model achieves state-of-the-art performance relative to recent methods for auditory, visual, and audiovisual recognition. The result shows that sharing one model across these tasks can coexist with strong task-specific performance. The contribution spans both model unification and ways of learning from unlabeled data, addressing the training process as well as the fragmented inference setup.
neurips-2024-unified-speech-recognition-.tldr: Unified training, pseudo-labeling, and self-supervised pretraining enable one model to achieve state-of-the-art LRS3 results across three speech-recognition input modes.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting can render realistic views efficiently, but extracting a clean surface from its point-based representation remains difficult. Existing approaches use predicted surface normals as geometric guidance. The paper identifies two problems: supervising rendered normals can update only Gaussian rotation, and normal predictions that disagree across views can introduce serious reconstruction artifacts.

VCR-GauS introduces a depth-normal regularizer that connects normals to other geometric parameters, allowing normal-based supervision to update the full geometry. A confidence term reduces the effect of inconsistencies between normal predictions from different viewpoints. The method also controls the size and distribution of Gaussians through a densification and splitting strategy, supporting more accurate surface modeling.

Compared with Gaussian-based baselines, experiments show better surface reconstruction while retaining competitive appearance quality. The authors also report faster training and rendering above 100 frames per second. These results connect improvements in geometric supervision to the practical goal of extracting better surfaces while preserving efficient rendering. The approach addresses both incomplete parameter updates and disagreement in the geometric guidance.
neurips-2024-vcr-gaus-view-consistent-de.tldr: VCR-GauS couples depth and normal supervision, handles cross-view inconsistency, and refines Gaussian placement to improve surface reconstruction while retaining fast rendering.

paragraphs: Visual Riddles tests whether vision and language models can connect subtle image cues with commonsense and world knowledge. Recognizing what is visible may be insufficient to explain a scene: a small contextual detail can make an otherwise ambiguous situation understandable. The benchmark is designed to probe that interpretive ability through questions about visual scenarios.

It contains 400 riddles, each with a distinct image generated by one of several text-to-image models. Every item includes a question, a ground-truth answer, a textual hint, and attribution. The benchmark also provides automatic evaluation tasks, making it possible to assess models at scale alongside the reported human evaluation.

The evaluation reveals a substantial gap: humans achieve 82% accuracy, while the leading tested model, Gemini-Pro-1.5, reaches 40%. These results identify difficulty with this collection of knowledge-dependent visual questions. The benchmark offers a resource for studying that gap and improving interpretation of complex scenes, with its findings grounded in the particular riddles and models evaluated.
neurips-2024-visual-riddles-a-commonsens.tldr: Visual Riddles exposes a large human–model accuracy gap on image questions that require commonsense, world knowledge, and subtle visual cues.

paragraphs: Sketchpad gives multimodal language models a workspace for drawing intermediate visual artifacts during reasoning. The motivation is that people use lines, marks, and sketches to make relationships easier to inspect and reduce demands on memory. The framework lets a model plan and reason using the visual material it creates, extending intermediate reasoning beyond text.

The drawing tools produce simple elements such as lines, boxes, and marks. Sketchpad can also call specialist vision models, using object detection to draw bounding boxes or segmentation to draw masks. These capabilities connect perception with the sketching process, allowing the model’s evolving visual workspace to incorporate information extracted from the image.

Across the evaluated mathematics and complex visual reasoning tasks, Sketchpad improves on strong base models without sketching. Reported average gains are 12.7% for mathematics and 8.6% for vision. GPT-4o with Sketchpad achieves state-of-the-art results on all evaluated tasks, including 80.3% on V*Bench, 83.9% on BLINK spatial reasoning, and 80.8% on visual correspondence. The findings support drawn artifacts as useful aids to multimodal reasoning.
neurips-2024-visual-sketchpad-sketching-.tldr: Sketchpad lets multimodal models draw and inspect visual reasoning aids, improving performance across the evaluated math and vision tasks.
